section.title: A Call to Rebuild the Temple
section.sectionRationale: The first dated oracle of the book, delivered on the first day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius, 520 BC. It is one complete unit: the LORD's rebuke of a people who panel their own houses while His house lies in ruins, His call to consider their ways and build, and the remnant's swift obedience under Zerubbabel and Joshua.
section.thesis: When the returned exiles put their own comfort before the house of God, the LORD confronts their misplaced priorities, calls them to consider their ways and build, and then stirs their hearts with the promise, I am with you.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the rebuke for a temple left in ruins; the call to consider their ways and rebuild for God's glory; and the remnant's obedience as the LORD stirs their spirit.

units.label: The rebuke: a house in ruins
units.note: these people say the time has not come

verses.text: In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, stating
that this is what the {{lordOfHosts|LORD of Hosts}} says: “These people say, ‘The time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD.’”
Then the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet, saying:
“Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in {{ruins|ruins}}?”

units.label: Consider your ways and build
units.note: you have planted much but harvested little

verses.text: Now this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “{{consider|Consider carefully your ways}}.

You have planted much but harvested little. You eat but never have enough. You drink but never have your fill. You put on clothes but never get warm. You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through.”
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Consider carefully your ways.
Go up into the hills, bring down lumber, and build the house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be {{glorified|glorified}}, says the LORD.

You expected much, but behold, it amounted to little. And what you brought home, I blew away. Why? declares the LORD of Hosts. Because My house still lies in ruins, while each of you is busy with his own house.
Therefore, on account of you the heavens have withheld their dew and the earth has withheld its crops.
I have summoned a drought on the fields and on the mountains, on the grain, new wine, and oil, and on whatever the ground yields, on man and beast, and on all the labor of your hands.”

Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as all the {{remnant|remnant}} of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God and the words of the prophet Haggai, because the LORD their God had sent him. So the people feared the LORD.
Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, delivered the message of the LORD to the people: “{{immanu|I am with you}},” declares the LORD.

So the LORD {{stir|stirred}} the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God,
on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.

lordOfHosts.gloss: The LORD of Hosts, or LORD of Armies. Tseva'ot means armies or hosts, the heavenly ranks and all the powers of creation. The title, which drums through Haggai fourteen times, presents the covenant God as the sovereign commander of every force in heaven and earth, more than able to fulfil what He promises to a small and struggling people.

ruins.gloss: Waste, desolate, laid in ruins. The same root can describe a dried up land or a devastated building. Haggai sets the ruined house of God against the people's finished, paneled houses, exposing where their true treasure lay.

consider.gloss: Literally, set your heart upon your ways. It is more than a passing thought; it is a summons to weigh life honestly before God, to trace the connection between spiritual neglect and empty results. Haggai repeats the call so it cannot be ignored.

glorified.gloss: To be heavy, weighty, honored, glorified. The root behind glory, kavod, carries the idea of weight and worth. God calls His people to build so that He may take pleasure in the house and display His weighty glory, the true purpose behind the timber and stone.

remnant.gloss: A remnant, remainder, those who are left. It names the small company that survived exile and returned to the land. The prophets often speak of a remnant preserved by grace through whom God keeps His promises alive.

immanu.gloss: I am with you. The great covenant assurance spoken to Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Joshua, and gathered up in the name Immanuel, God with us. Here it turns fearful, discouraged builders into a working people, for the presence of God is their strength.

stir.gloss: To rouse, awaken, stir up. The LORD stirs the spirit of leaders and people alike, so their obedience is not mere willpower but the fruit of God awakening them. Human response and divine grace meet in the same moment.

basic.context: About eighteen years after the first exiles came home from Babylon, the temple of God still lay in ruins. The people had grown comfortable, finishing their own paneled houses while God's house sat as a weedy foundation. In 520 BC God raises up the prophet Haggai, who tells them plainly why nothing is going right: they have put themselves first and God's house last.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened, on a datable day in history, and it teaches a lasting lesson about priorities. It is not a rule that every believer must build a physical building; it is a call to put God and His purposes first, and a warning that a life built around our own comfort leaves us strangely empty. Haggai twice says, consider your ways, and that call still lands on us.
basic.originalLanguages: God is called the LORD of Hosts, the commander of every army in heaven and earth, so His call carries real weight. He tells them to consider their ways, literally to set their hearts on their ways, to weigh their lives honestly. He wants the house built so He may be glorified, a word that means weighty, honored. And He stirs their spirit, awakening them to obey.
basic.typology: The temple was the place where God dwelt among His people. It points forward to Jesus, who is God dwelling with us, and to the church as God's living temple. The call to build God's house foreshadows the greater building work God does in Christ, gathering a people as His dwelling by the Spirit.
basic.christ: The whole point of the temple was that God would dwell with His people and be glorified. Jesus is the true temple, God present in the flesh, and He said something greater than the temple is here. The rebuilding of a humble house in Haggai's day was one small step in the long story that leads to Christ, in whom God fully dwells and through whom we are made His temple.
basic.god: God cares about His glory and about being first in the lives of His people, not out of vanity but because we were made for Him. He disciplines with hard providences to wake us up, yet the moment His people turn, He speaks the tender words, I am with you, and stirs their hearts to obey. He is both the God who confronts and the God who comes near.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus says to seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest will follow, Matthew 6:33. Paul calls the church the temple of God, 1 Corinthians 3:16. And the Lord promises never to leave nor forsake His people, Hebrews 13:5, the same assurance Haggai brings.
basic.oneStory: Haggai's call to rebuild is one thread in the Bible's long story of God dwelling with His people, from the garden, to the tabernacle, to the temple, to Christ, to the church, and finally to the new creation where God dwells with us forever. Rebuilding this modest house kept that story moving toward its fulfilment in Jesus.

context.literary:
Haggai 1 is a compact piece of prophetic rhetoric with a clear frame. The opening verse supplies a full date, the second year of Darius, first day of the sixth month, and names the two leaders addressed. The closing verse, 1:15, supplies a second date, the twenty-fourth day of the same month, and the work begins. The twenty three days between the two dates are the whole story of the chapter: a word received, a word obeyed. The book as a whole is organised by such dates, 1:1, 2:1, 2:10 and 2:20, and here the frame turns a prophetic oracle into a record of a moment in history.

Inside the frame the chapter alternates between speech and report. Verses 2 to 11 give God's case in three movements. First comes the quotation of the people's excuse, verse 2, and the sharp question in reply, verse 4. Then the commands: 'Consider carefully your ways' appears at verse 5 and again at verse 7, so that the charge about harvest, verse 6, and the order to build, verse 8, are each introduced by the same summons. Finally the explanation, verses 9 to 11, gives the 'why' with 'because My house still lies in ruins.' The reader meets the same cause and effect twice, first as experience and then as a verdict.

A wordplay holds the argument together. The temple lies in 'ruins' in verse 4, a word whose letters in Hebrew are close to the word for 'drought' that God summons in verse 11. The sound of the one word is answered by the sound of the other, so that the dryness of the fields is set beside the desolation of the house. The piling up of short clauses in verse 6, planted, eat, drink, clothe, earn, each ending in failure, makes the lack felt rather than argued. Then verses 12 to 15 shift to narrative, and the cadence changes from accusation to action.
context.historical:
The date in 1:1 is late August 520 BC, in the reign of the Persian king Darius I. The exiles had returned in 538 BC under Cyrus's decree, Ezra 1:1 to 4, and had set up the altar and begun worship, Ezra 3:1 to 3. They laid the foundation of the temple in the second year after their arrival, Ezra 3:8 to 10, and then work stopped under pressure from neighbours who wrote to the king, Ezra 4:4 to 5 and 4:23 to 24. The building stood at a standstill 'until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia,' exactly the year of Haggai. So about sixteen years separated the foundation from the oracle.

The people addressed were a small community in a modest province. The governor, Zerubbabel, was a grandson of King Jehoiachin, 1 Chronicles 3:17 to 19 and Matthew 1:12, so the line of David still had a representative, though not a throne. The word for 'governor' is a Persian administrative term, a reminder that Judah was a subject province. Joshua, also called Jeshua in Ezra, was high priest, and the BSB footnote on 1:1 explains that his father's name is a variant, Jehozadak or Jozadak. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah are recorded together in Ezra 5:1 to 2 as the voices that restarted the work.

The excuse 'the time has not yet come' probably reflects a calculation. Jeremiah had spoken of seventy years of Babylon, Jeremiah 29:10, and counted from the destruction of the temple in 586 BC, seventy years ends in 516 BC. Some of the people may have been waiting out that period. Whatever lay behind the words, the paneled houses of verse 4 reveal the real difficulty. The word 'paneled' is used of fine cedar work in the palaces of Solomon, 1 Kings 7:3 and 7, and in Jeremiah's rebuke of King Jehoiakim for his own paneled palace, Jeremiah 22:14. Ordinary families had built to a standard that once belonged to kings. Once the work resumed, the temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius, Ezra 6:14 to 15.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs within the long Old Testament story of the place where God dwells. The tabernacle was built at God's command and filled with His glory, Exodus 40:34 to 35. Solomon's temple was dedicated with the same filling cloud, 1 Kings 8:10 to 11. The prophets before the exile spoke of God abandoning a house His people had polluted, and the temple was burned in 586 BC. Haggai takes up the story at the point where the community is once again free to restore the place, and where God asks them to do it.

The covenant background to verses 6 and 9 to 11 is the blessings and curses of the law. Deuteronomy 28:38 to 40 warns of sowing much and harvesting little and of vineyards and olive trees that give nothing, and Leviticus 26:19 to 20 speaks of a sky like iron and land that yields no produce. Haggai does not invent a new theology of hard times; he reminds the people that the God of the covenant had already said what neglect of Him would look like. The words in 1:6 and 1:9 return, after the exile, to the structure of Moses' warnings.

The stirring of the spirits in verse 14 recalls Ezra 1:5, where God stirred the spirit of those who went up to build, so that the same divine work lies behind both the first return and the renewed work. The New Testament draws on the temple theme in several ways. Jesus calls His own body the temple, John 2:19 to 21, and tells the Pharisees that something greater than the temple is here, Matthew 12:6. Paul tells the church, 'you yourselves are God's temple, and God's Spirit dwells in you,' 1 Corinthians 3:16, and Ephesians 2:21 to 22 describes believers growing into a holy temple in the Lord. Haggai's call to build is a link in this chain.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Haggai means to do something sharper than teach a principle. He wants a particular community to put down their tools in their own houses and pick them up on God's. The strategy is to take the people's private reading of their circumstances and give it a new interpretation. They have seen scarcity and concluded that the time is wrong; he tells them that the scarcity is itself the sign that their priorities are wrong. The question in verse 4 is meant to sting, and the repeated command to consider is meant to make them go and look at their own barns and clothing.

He also means to restore the dignity of the work. A foundation that has lain for sixteen years and a handful of poor people have little to boast of, and he does not flatter them. What he gives them instead is the word of God, the leaders' obedience, and the promise of verse 13. The reader is meant to see that the work matters because God has called it and is with those who do it, not because the building will impress anyone.

There is a pastoral tone beneath the rebuke. The two leaders are addressed first and named with their fathers, and the people as a whole are called a remnant, verse 12. Haggai sees them as the beginning of a restored community and not only as offenders. The correction is meant to get them moving, and the report of the speed with which they obey, in under four weeks, is the proof that the message did its work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a dated command to a specific people about a specific building. Nowhere does it tell later generations to construct a temple, and the New Testament says that God no longer lives in temples made by hands, Acts 7:48 to 49 and 17:24. To turn the passage into a command to put up church buildings would miss both the original setting and the later teaching on where God now dwells.

It does not prescribe a simple formula either. Haggai 1:6 and 1:10 to 11 should not be read as a rule that every poor harvest or lean year is a punishment for neglecting God. Job's story and Jesus' remark about the tower of Siloam, Luke 13:1 to 5, forbid that inference. Haggai interprets one situation with the authority of a prophet who has the word of the LORD; later readers have no such authority to read their neighbours' trouble as judgment.

What carries over is the pattern. A community can be busy with its own houses while God's purposes wait. God wants honest examination, 'Consider carefully your ways.' He is pleased when His people turn the work of their hands toward His kingdom, and He promises His presence to those who obey. Jesus' call to seek first the kingdom, Matthew 6:33, and Paul's complaint that everyone looks after their own interests, Philippians 2:21, show the same concerns in new settings.

debates.question: What did the people mean by 'The time has not yet come'?

views.label: They were waiting for the seventy years to end
views.case: Jeremiah 25:11 and 29:10 fixed seventy years for Babylon's rule and the exile. If the people reckoned from the destruction of the temple in 586 BC, the end of that period was 516 BC, still some years away. Their reply would then be a kind of reverence: they were not neglecting the temple but waiting for God's time.

views.label: They were using hardship and opposition as an excuse
views.case: Ezra 4:4 to 5 records that opponents discouraged the builders and bribed officials against them, and that work then ceased. The people had a reasonable fear of Persian displeasure. Haggai's rebuke fits a community that used difficulty as a reason to wait, while building comfortable houses for themselves.

debates.bearing: Haggai does not engage the calendar argument at all; he points to the paneled houses and the empty harvests. Whether the excuse was timing or fear, it was a reason that served their comfort, and the prophet answers it by reminding them that God's house comes first.

debates.question: Who is the 'messenger of the LORD' in verse 13, and what does the title mean?

views.label: Haggai himself as a prophet
views.case: The verse says that Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, delivered the message. The Hebrew word for messenger is the same word used for angels and appears in the name Malachi, 'my messenger.' Prophets are elsewhere called the LORD's messengers, as in 2 Chronicles 36:15 to 16, which says God sent word by His messengers.

views.label: A title that reminds the people why they must listen
views.case: Verse 12 has already said that the people obeyed 'because the LORD their God had sent him.' The title in verse 13 then confirms that Haggai's authority is not his own, and it gives the short message 'I am with you' the weight of a sent word.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together: Haggai is a human prophet, and his office is that of a messenger. The point for later readers is that the people received the word as God's word, 1 Thessalonians 2:13 describes the same kind of hearing, and that is why it changed them.

debates.question: Is 'I am with you' a reward for obedience or the cause of it?

views.label: A reward that follows obedience
views.case: The order of the text puts obedience first, verse 12, then the promise, verse 13, then the work, verse 14. The promise can be read as God's response to their repentance.

views.label: A grace that makes obedience possible
views.case: The same verse 14 says that the LORD 'stirred' their spirits, and the work followed the stirring. On this reading the promise and the stirring come from God before the work is done.

debates.bearing: Scripture holds both together, as in Philippians 2:12 to 13, where believers work out their salvation because God is at work in them. The promise is sure whether it is the first or the second step.

study.originalLanguages:
The title 'governor' in 1:1 and 1:14 is a Persian administrative word, a reminder that Judah was a province in an empire. Haggai also uses unusual care with names: 'Joshua son of Jehozadak' is the Hebrew form of the name Jeshua, which is Yeshua, the same as Jesus. The BSB footnote notes that Jehozadak is a variant of Jozadak. In the next chapters Zechariah will place this Joshua in a vision with the Branch, Zechariah 3 and 6:12 to 13, so the name carries more weight than a first reading suggests.

In verse 4 the question 'Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses?' puts the pronoun 'you' in emphatic position, 'you yourselves.' The word 'paneled' comes from a root meaning to cover or panel, used of the finest cedar work, 1 Kings 7:3 and 7, and of the palace of Jehoiakim in Jeremiah 22:14. The people had built homes in the style of kings. The final word of the verse, 'ruins,' is a near homophone of the word for drought in verse 11, a play the Hebrew reader would hear at once: the house lies in ruin, so the land is given to drought.

Verse 6 is written in a rhythm of failure. The first line says literally 'you have sown much, and brought in little,' using a word for abundance followed by a word for smallness. The next lines use infinitive forms, eat, drink, clothe, and each ends with the negative, 'but not to satisfaction.' The picture of wages put into 'a bag pierced through' is of a bag with holes, a purse that leaks out the money as fast as it is filled. It is one of the most vivid images of futile labour in the Old Testament.

In verse 9 the phrase 'I blew away' is literally 'I blew on it.' The word is used of breathing out, and here it means that whatever the people brought home, God blew it away like chaff. The breath that gives life in Genesis 2:7 is here turned against the harvest the people had counted on.

In verse 12 the leaders and people 'obeyed the voice of the LORD their God,' a Hebrew idiom that means literally 'listened to the voice.' The same expression appears in Deuteronomy 28:1, where listening to the voice is the condition of blessing.

Finally, the promise in verse 13, 'I am with you,' is only two words in Hebrew, followed by the divine declaration. The same promise was given to Jacob in Genesis 28:15, to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:12, and to Joshua in Joshua 1:5. Haggai's hearers are given the promise that had accompanied every great task in Israel's story.

typology.type: The house of God lying in ruins, Haggai 1:4
typology.fulfillment: The ruined temple is a picture of God's dwelling neglected by His people. In the Gospels Jesus finds the temple used for trade and drives out the sellers, Matthew 21:12 to 13, and then speaks of His own body as the temple that will be destroyed and raised, John 2:19 to 21. The type finds its answer in Christ, in whom God's presence is not a building to be rebuilt in a lifetime but a person raised in three days. The type falls short because Haggai's temple needed constant upkeep and could be neglected; the temple of Christ's body cannot be destroyed in the end.

typology.type: Zerubbabel and Joshua, governor and high priest, Haggai 1:1 and 1:12
typology.fulfillment: Two leaders, one of David's line and one of the priestly line, stand together in the work. Zechariah sees them as pictures of a coming Branch who will build the temple of the LORD and 'be a priest on His throne,' with 'peaceful counsel between the two,' Zechariah 6:12 to 13. In Jesus the offices of king and priest meet in one person, Hebrews 8:1 to 2. The type falls short because the two men were separate and mortal and the governor never sat on a throne; in Christ both offices belong to one who lives forever.

The remnant begins to build God's house with their own hands. Paul tells the Corinthians that they are God's building and God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:9 and 16, and Ephesians 2:20 to 22 describes the household of God built on Christ the cornerstone. Peter calls believers 'living stones' being built into a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5. The correspondence is that God again gathers a community to be His dwelling. The escalation is that the house is now made of people from every nation, indwelt by the Spirit, and the type falls short in that Haggai's stones were quarried from the hills, while Christ's stones are living.

typology.type: Drought withheld, the covenant curse, Haggai 1:10 to 11
typology.fulfillment: The withheld dew and the failing crops correspond to the curses of the law. Galatians 3:13 says that Christ redeemed His people from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for them, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The type shows what neglect of God deserves; the cross shows who bore the cost. The correspondence falls short because Haggai's drought was temporal and local, while the curse borne by Christ is the full weight of sin.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the theme of God's dwelling. The reason Haggai cares about the house is that the house is the place where God lives among His people, and Haggai 1:13, 'I am with you,' is the promise that every temple was meant to carry. John writes that the Word 'became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and the verb he uses carries the sense of pitching a tent, recalling the tabernacle. Colossians 2:9 says that 'in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.' What the temple gave in picture, Christ gives in person.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the two leaders. Zerubbabel, in the line of David, and Joshua the high priest, together carry the people into the work. Zechariah, working alongside Haggai, takes this pairing and points beyond it to the Branch who 'will build the temple of the LORD' and 'sit on His throne and rule' as a priest, Zechariah 6:12 to 13. The author of Hebrews says that Jesus is the high priest who 'ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man,' Hebrews 8:1 to 2, and that He has 'greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3. The builder of God's house is greater than any house.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The people in Haggai's day put their own houses first. Jesus, who had no place to lay His head, Matthew 8:20, said, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me,' John 4:34. He cleansed the temple with the words 'My house will be called a house of prayer,' Matthew 21:12 to 13, and He declared that 'something greater than the temple is here,' Matthew 12:6. Where Israel's builders had to be stirred, He came of His own accord.

It leads to Christ through the promise of presence. Matthew ends with 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, the same words as Haggai 1:13 in the mouth of the risen Lord. The people who build in obedience are not building alone. Believers who now are 'living stones' in the house that Christ is raising, 1 Peter 2:5, are doing the work of Haggai's remnant on a larger scale.

A caution is needed. Haggai himself does not name the Messiah in this chapter; he calls for a building and promises God's presence. The New Testament takes the temple, the leaders and the promise and shows how they find their answer in Jesus. The links above rest on its own use of the temple theme, not on reading Christ into every detail of the text.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who speaks plainly about priorities. He does not let the people's excuse stand, and He quotes it back to them, 'These people say,' verse 2. The God of Haggai notices what His people say to each other and weighs it. He is also a God of evidence: the failures of verse 6 are not hidden from Him, and He tells the people that He is behind them. Nothing in the world is outside His governance, neither the dew that falls nor the drought that comes, verses 10 and 11.

He is a God who seeks glory, and the text is careful about why. 'That I may take pleasure in it and be glorified,' verse 8, is not vanity. The whole of Scripture teaches that the creature finds its good in the glory of its Maker, as in Isaiah 43:7 and 1 Corinthians 10:31. When God asks to be honoured He is asking His people to live in line with reality, and so the demand for His glory is also the offer of what they need most.

He disciplines in order to restore. The language of covenant blessing and curse, Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26, shows that the lean years were not random. Yet the purpose of the rebuke is that the people will change course, and God speaks 'Consider carefully your ways' twice before He issues any threat. Hebrews 12:5 to 11 describes the same pattern of a Father who disciplines those He loves.

He is a God of tender nearness. The shortest sentence in the chapter is the most important: 'I am with you.' It comes to a people who have just been rebuked, and it comes before the work is done. The God who confronts is the same God who comes close, and He treats them as a remnant to be rebuilt and not as a failure to be discarded. Notice that the promise of presence is not the reward at the end of the work but the ground under it.

He is a God who works in the human heart. The verb 'stirred' in verse 14 shows that obedience itself is something He gives. He had stirred the spirit of Cyrus, Ezra 1:1, and the spirit of the exiles, Ezra 1:5, and now He stirs the leaders and the people. Philippians 2:13 says it is God who works in believers 'to will and to act.'

For worship, the chapter teaches a believer to ask what has been put ahead of God's work, and to hear in the question not only a charge but an invitation. God does not rebuke His people to leave them in ruins, but to build them as His house. The right response is to consider, to obey, and to hear the promise with gratitude.

crossReferences.note: Records that Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and that Zerubbabel and Jeshua then rose up and began to rebuild, with the prophets helping them. It is the historical report of the same events and shows that the prophecy was received and put to work.

The covenant warns of sowing much and harvesting little, of vineyards and olives that give no fruit. These are the very conditions Haggai describes in 1:6 and 1:9, and the verses show that the prophet is applying the law of Moses and not inventing a theory.

The LORD says He will make the sky like iron and the land like bronze so that the land will not yield its produce. It matches the drought of Haggai 1:10 to 11 and shows that the withheld dew is a covenant sign.

The prophet condemns King Jehoiakim for building himself a spacious palace paneled in cedar while he neglected justice. It shows the same word for paneling that Haggai uses in 1:4, and so reveals how the people had adopted royal standards for their own comfort.

Zechariah, speaking in the same years, recalls the day the foundation was laid and promises that the remnant will no longer be treated as before. The seed, vine and dew will be given as an inheritance. It supplies the encouragement that follows Haggai's rebuke.

God stirs the spirit of the heads of Judah and Benjamin and the priests to go up and build the house of the LORD. It shows that the stirring in Haggai 1:14 is the same kind of divine work that began the first return.

Jesus tells His disciples to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things will be added. It states the principle Haggai applied to a rebuilding project, that God's priority comes first and daily needs follow.

Jesus says something greater than the temple is here. It shows that the temple Haggai urged the people to build was always a pointer to a person, and that He has come in whom God's presence is fully found.

Paul says that God works in believers to will and to act according to His good purpose. It gives the New Testament account of what Haggai 1:14 shows when God stirs the spirit of the leaders and the people to begin work.
Paul tells the church that they are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in them. The call to build the house in Haggai finds its New Testament answer in the community in which the Spirit lives.
God says, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.' It echoes the promise 'I am with you' in Haggai 1:13 and shows that the assurance given to the remnant stands for every believer.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with God dwelling with humanity in a garden, Genesis 2 and 3, and the loss of that dwelling is the central tragedy of Genesis. From the moment of exile from Eden, the Bible traces how God makes a way to live among His people again: the tabernacle in the wilderness, Exodus 25:8, the temple of Solomon, 1 Kings 8, and then, after judgment, the humble rebuilding in Haggai's day. The rebuilt house is a step along the same road.

Haggai answers a question the exile had left hanging. When the glory departed and the temple burned, did God still intend to live among His people? The call to rebuild, with its promise 'I am with you,' says yes. The returned community is small and poor, yet it is the continuation of the line of promise that runs from Abraham through David. The house they raised stood until the days of Herod, and in it the infant Jesus was presented, Luke 2:22 to 32.

The chapter also shows how the story moves: God stirs a people from within and works through ordinary leaders and unremarkable labour. The first return was a small beginning, and so was the rebuilding. This pattern of small beginnings and large outcomes runs through the whole Bible, from the seed of the woman in Genesis 3:15 to the child in a manger and the mustard seed of the kingdom.

From here the story moves to Christ, who says that the temple of His body will be raised, John 2:19, and then to the church, a temple of living stones, 1 Peter 2:5. The Spirit dwells in a people from every nation, 1 Corinthians 3:16. The story ends with a vision in which there is no temple at all: John sees no temple in the city, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The house that Haggai's hearers raised stone by stone gives way to the dwelling it was always promising, where 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. The priorities of Haggai's day are thus caught up in a larger priority, that God would be with His people forever, and every obedient act of building that serves it is part of the one story.

sermon.title: Build God's House (Haggai Part 1)
sermon.why: From Legge's expository series Majoring On The Minors: Haggai, this message works through the whole of Haggai 1:1-15, unfolding the rebuke for procrastination, the reaping of poverty, and the renewal of purpose, with clear application to putting God first. A sound, orthodox exposition of this exact passage.

quiz.q: Why were the people's efforts leaving them empty and frustrated?

options.text: They had put their own comfort first and left God's house in ruins.
options.note: Haggai ties their fruitless lives directly to neglecting God's house and His glory.

options.text: They were simply going through a run of bad weather and poor harvests.
options.note: The hard times were real, but Haggai reveals their spiritual root: misplaced priorities.

options.text: They had not worked hard enough on their farms.
options.note: The problem was not lack of effort but a heart that put self before God.

options.text: God had simply abandoned them for no reason.
options.note: God had not abandoned them; He was calling them back and promising, I am with you.

quiz.q: What does the repeated call consider your ways mean?

options.text: Set your heart honestly on your life before God and trace the connection between neglect and emptiness.
options.note: The Hebrew sim lev means to weigh life seriously, not a passing thought.

options.text: Feel a little guilty and then carry on as before.
options.note: It calls for real reckoning that leads to change, not mere fleeting guilt.

options.text: Make a better financial plan for the year.
options.note: It is a spiritual summons about priorities before God, not budgeting advice.

options.text: Ignore the past and just think positively.
options.note: It is precisely a call to examine the past honestly before God.

quiz.q: Why did God want the temple rebuilt?

options.text: So that He might take pleasure in it and be glorified among His people.
options.note: Verse 8 gives the reason: that I may take pleasure in it and be glorified.

options.text: Mainly to give the people a big construction project to keep busy.
options.note: The work mattered, but its purpose was God's pleasure and glory, not busyness.

options.text: To make the nation wealthy and powerful again.
options.note: The aim was God's glory and presence, not national prosperity for its own sake.

options.text: Because God needed a building to live in.
options.note: God is not contained by buildings; the temple displayed His presence and glory.

quiz.q: What finally moved the people to obey and build?

options.text: The LORD stirred their spirit after the promise, I am with you.
options.note: Verses 13-14 show God's presence and His stirring grace behind their obedience.

options.text: They felt too ashamed not to do something.
options.note: Conviction played a part, but the text credits God stirring their spirit.

options.text: The governor forced them to work.
options.note: Zerubbabel led, but it was the LORD who stirred leaders and people alike.

options.text: The weather suddenly improved.
options.note: The turning point was God's word and His stirring, not a change in weather.

quiz.q: How does the temple in Haggai point to Christ?

options.text: It was the place of God's dwelling and glory, fulfilled in Jesus, the true temple, God with us.
options.note: Jesus is the greater temple where God dwells among us, John 2:19-21; Matthew 12:6.

options.text: It shows that God only ever wanted grand buildings.
options.note: The building served God's presence; that presence comes fully in Christ, not in architecture.

options.text: It proves believers must build literal temples today.
options.note: The church is now God's temple; the call is to God's dwelling, not a building program.

options.text: It has no connection to Jesus at all.
options.note: The whole temple theme leads to Christ, in whom God dwells bodily.

questions: The people finished their own paneled houses while God's house lay in ruins. Where might your own comfort be quietly crowding out God's rightful first place?
Twice God says, consider your ways. If you set your heart honestly on your life right now, where do you see emptiness that a reordering of priorities might address?
God tied their frustration to their neglect of Him. Are there frustrations in your life that might be an invitation to return to Him rather than merely a problem to fix?
Only four weeks passed between Haggai's word and the start of the work. Is there some obedience you have been putting off with the excuse that the time has not yet come?
God's tender word, I am with you, turned discouraged people into willing builders. How would truly believing that God is with you change the work in front of you this week?

translationNotes.note: The LORD of Hosts renders YHWH tseva'ot, the LORD of Armies, a title used repeatedly in Haggai to stress God's sovereign power over all heaven and earth.
Consider carefully your ways renders the Hebrew idiom set your heart upon your ways, a call to serious self-examination before God.
A bag pierced through, or a bag with holes, vividly pictures wages that slip away and never satisfy, whether through scarcity or inflation.
